note: Weaknesses deliberately designed into case study 2, recorded before the engine was first run. 'expected' is the finding id the current rule base should produce, or null when no rule covers it (a known gap). This is the design key, not the manual STRIDE baseline used in evaluation.

weaknesses.description: Appointment lookup checks the token but not ownership (IDOR / BOLA).
Reminder sends are not logged.
Execution role not scoped to least privilege.
HL7 v2 messages parsed without validation.
Legacy interface engine runs as root.
No dependency scanning on the legacy engine.
Lab results (PHI) sent as HL7 over plain-TCP MLLP.
Integration engine calls the FHIR service unauthenticated, trusting VPN origin.
No access logging on the clinical documents bucket.
Queue holding patient reminder data is not encrypted at rest.
Cache of FHIR responses not encrypted at rest.
Single-node cache in front of the FHIR service.
Redis traffic unencrypted inside the VPC (same trust boundary).
Admin console exposed to the internet behind basic auth.
No rate limiting on the admin login (brute force).
PHI (name, appointment type) sent to a third-party SMS provider; encrypted and authenticated, but violates data minimisation.
Pseudonymised data is labelled 'internal' but remains personal data (GDPR Recital 26); re-identification risk at the research partner.
Admin console writes to the EHR database directly, bypassing the FHIR service's authorisation layer.
Single on-prem interface engine; lab feed stops if it fails. D-03 covers stateful stores only.
Engine accepts MLLP connections without authenticating the sender; S-01 only covers internet-facing components.
